definition.text: Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth.

facts.text: It can be measured at several levels, such as the variety of genes, of species and of whole ecosystems.
Biologists most often describe it as the totality of genes, species and ecosystems of a region.
Life is not spread evenly: there is more diversity in the tropics, helped by the warm climate and high plant growth near the equator.
Tropical forests cover less than one-fifth of Earth's land yet hold about 50% of the world's species.
Estimates by Mora et al. (2011) put the number of species at about 8.7 million on land and 2.2 million in the ocean.
Human activities are causing ongoing biodiversity loss, often called the Holocene or sixth mass extinction; clearing habitat for farming is a key cause.
Many studies link greater plant species diversity to useful results such as higher fodder and crop yields.
In 2019 the IPBES Global Assessment stated that the state of nature had deteriorated at an unprecedented and accelerating rate.

definition.text: The pattern in which the number of species rises from the poles toward the tropics.

facts.text: Places at lower latitudes generally hold more species than places at higher latitudes.
Several factors may contribute, but the underlying one behind many of them is the higher average temperature at the equator.
The rule has exceptions: parasites do not seem to follow it, and soil bacterial diversity peaks in temperate zones.

definition.text: The link between how varied life is in a place and the benefits that place gives people.

facts.text: Many claims have been made about biodiversity boosting ecosystem services; some are validated, some are wrong and some lack enough evidence.
Biodiversity supports regulating services that make ecosystems more stable, functional and adaptable.
Different plants living together can play complementary roles, such as cycling nutrients and regulating water, which steadies ecosystems under climate stress; this is called niche complementarity.

definition.text: Ecosystem services are the many benefits people get from ecosystems.

facts.text: Examples include pollination of crops, clean air and water, breakdown of wastes and flood control.
They are vital for human well-being, giving direct and indirect benefits such as clean water, food and climate regulation.
The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, a United Nations initiative of the early 2000s, popularised sorting them into four groups: provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural.
New York City restored its Catskill watershed for an estimated $1–1.5 billion instead of building a filtration plant estimated at $6–8 billion plus $300 million a year to run.
Economists value these services in money using methods such as avoided cost, replacement cost, travel cost, hedonic pricing and contingent valuation.
A 1997 study estimated the value of the world's ecosystem services and natural capital at US$16–54 trillion per year, averaging US$33 trillion.
Payments for ecosystem services reward farmers or landowners for managing their land so that it provides an ecological service.
The term 'environmental services' appeared in a 1970 report; later 'ecosystem services' became the standard term in the scientific literature.

title: Ecosystem service categories

definition.text: The ways ecosystem services are sorted into groups, most famously the four groups of the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment.

facts.text: The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment uses regulating, provisioning, cultural and supporting services, with supporting services the base for the other three.
An ecosystem need not offer all four kinds at once, but people usually benefit from a mix of them.
Some services touch nearby people directly, like fresh water or food, while others act through general conditions, like climate or erosion regulation.
To avoid counting the same benefit twice, The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity replaced supporting services with habitat services.
The Common International Classification for Ecosystem Services keeps cultural and provisioning services but merges regulating and habitat services into regulation and maintenance services.
Provisioning services are the products obtained from ecosystems, such as food, fresh water, wood, fibre and fuel.
Regulating services are benefits from the regulation of ecosystem processes, such as climate control, carbon sequestration, flood control and disease regulation.
Supporting services, such as nutrient cycling, primary production and soil formation, allow the other services to exist.

notes: Phrase concept; Ecosystem service#Categories (seeded in nature-as-the-economy-s-foundation) may cover the same ground.

definition.text: The products people obtain from ecosystems, also called ecosystem goods.

facts.text: They include food such as crops, seafood, game and spices.
They also include raw materials such as lumber, skins, fuelwood, fodder and fertilizer.
Global production and trade of all major wood-based products reached their highest recorded values in 2018.

definition.text: The benefits people get from nature keeping ecosystem processes in check, such as climate, water and pests.

facts.text: Examples are carbon sequestration, breaking down and detoxifying wastes, and controlling pests and diseases.
Bee pollination is needed for 15–30% of U.S. food production.
Wetlands hold large amounts of water and release it slowly, making floods less likely; mangroves protect shorelines from erosion.

definition.text: The background services, such as nutrient cycling and soil formation, that make all other ecosystem services possible.

facts.text: Their effects on people are indirect and play out over long periods.
They include nutrient cycling, primary production, soil formation and providing habitat.
Primary production makes the organic matter that forms the base of all food webs and also releases oxygen.

title: Cultural services

definition.text: The non-material benefits of nature, such as recreation, beauty, learning and spiritual meaning.

facts.text: They are hard to put in money terms.
They include ecotourism and outdoor sports, the use of nature in art and national symbols, and its religious or heritage value.
Critics argue that cultural values attach to unique landscapes and ways of seeing, not to measurable ecosystem properties.

contested_note: Scholars disagree over whether cultural values can be fitted into the ecosystem services approach at all.

definition.text: Natural capital is the world's stock of natural resources, including rocks, soils, air, water and all living things.

facts.text: It stretches the economic idea of capital, meaning resources that let you produce more resources, to the goods and services nature provides.
A well-kept forest or river can supply new trees or fish indefinitely, while overuse can permanently shrink timber or fish stocks.
Some natural capital assets give people free goods and services, often called ecosystem services, which underpin the economy and society.
Older economics classed nature as 'land' with a fixed supply, but natural capital can be improved or degraded by people over time.
The term was first used in 1973 by E. F. Schumacher in Small Is Beautiful and developed by founders of ecological economics such as Herman Daly and Robert Costanza.
Its values are not counted in national income accounts or GDP and have no prices, because they lie mostly outside markets.
The OECD sees natural capital as three main categories: natural resource stocks, land and ecosystems.
When businesses or people damage nature without being held to account, the harmed nature is called unpriced natural capital.

definition.text: A 2012 pledge by finance-sector leaders to build natural capital into their products and reporting.

facts.text: It was launched at the Rio+20 summit in Brazil in June 2012.
Signed by 40 CEOs, it aimed to include natural capital in loans, equity, fixed income and insurance, and in accounting and reporting.
One aim was to increase understanding of how businesses depend on natural capital assets.

definition.text: A standard framework, released in 2016, that helps organisations identify, measure and value their impacts and dependencies on natural capital.

facts.text: It was released in July 2016 by the Natural Capital Coalition, now the Capitals Coalition.
It brings existing tools together so organisations can include nature in strategic and operational decisions.
It was developed by 38 organisations and is free to use under a Creative Commons licence.

definition.text: The international statistical standard (SEEA) for measuring the environment and how it relates to the economy.

facts.text: Environmental-economic accounts track both the economy's impacts on the environment and the environment's contribution to the economy.
The SEEA Central Framework was published in its final form in February 2014.
In March 2021 the UN Statistical Commission adopted the SEEA Ecosystem Accounting standard, covering ecosystem extent, condition and services in physical and money terms.
It is a satellite system of the UN System of National Accounts, so it uses the SNA's definitions and rules and the two sets of figures share boundaries.

title: Natural capital valuation debate

definition.text: The argument over whether nature and its free services should be given a money value.

facts.text: Measuring the parts of natural capital is fairly straightforward, but putting a money value on them has proved contentious.
Columnist George Monbiot derided valuation as trying to compare things that cannot be compared, calling the figures 'marmalade'.
Critics add that cultural values cannot carry a dollar amount, so valuation leaves parts of nature out.
Defenders say valuation puts the environment on a fairer footing against commercial pressures and is not the same as turning nature into money.

contested_note: Critics reject monetary valuation of nature while defenders say it gives the environment fairer weight in decisions.

definition.text: An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with their non-living surroundings, linked by flows of energy and nutrients.

facts.text: Living (biotic) parts are things like plants; non-living (abiotic) parts are things like soil.
Plants bring energy in through photosynthesis; animals move matter and energy by eating plants and each other; decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients.
Outside factors such as climate shape an ecosystem's structure without being affected by it, while inside factors such as decomposition and the species present both shape and respond to it.
Ecosystems are always recovering from past disturbances; the ability to absorb a shock and keep the same basic function is called ecological resilience.
They can range in size over ten orders of magnitude, from the surface of a rock to the surface of the planet.
The term was first used in 1935 by British ecologist Arthur Tansley; Arthur Roy Clapham coined the word at his request.
Ecosystems provide goods such as water, food, fuel and medicinal plants, and services such as clean air and water, oxygen and crop pollination.
Many are degraded by soil loss, pollution, habitat fragmentation and invasive species; one that has lost its defining features is called collapsed.

definition.text: The tangible, material products of ecosystems, such as water, food, fuel, building material and medicinal plants.

facts.text: They also include less tangible items like tourism and recreation, and wild genes used to improve domestic species.
They are set apart from ecosystem services, which are improvements in the condition or location of things of value.

title: Anthropocene

definition.text: The Anthropocene is a name for the period in which humanity has become a force that changes the whole planet.

facts.text: It was proposed as a new geological epoch after the Holocene but was rejected as such in 2024 by the ICS and IUGS.
The vote failed not because human impact was dismissed but because the epoch could not be pinned down geologically; the 1950 start date was judged prone to recency bias.
Proposed start dates range from the Neolithic Revolution, 12,000–15,000 years ago, to as recently as the 1960s.
Eugene F. Stoermer first used the term informally in the 1980s; Paul J. Crutzen popularised it.
Human effects on biodiversity are a main feature; extinction rates may be 100 to 1000 times the normal background rate, though the exact rate is disputed.
Rising atmospheric carbon dioxide, mostly from burning coal, oil and gas, is one geological sign of human activity.
The name joins Greek words meaning 'human' and 'new'.

contested_note: Whether the Anthropocene is a valid formal geological unit is disputed, and it was voted down as an epoch in 2024.

title: Anthropocene start-date debate

definition.text: The disagreement over when the human-shaped era of Earth's history began.

facts.text: Crutzen proposed the Industrial Revolution; Lovelock proposed the first Newcomen steam engine in 1712.
In 2019 the Anthropocene Working Group proposed the mid-20th century, when population, industry and farm chemicals surged and atomic tests left radioactive debris in sediments.
William Ruddiman argued it began about 8,000 years ago with farming and settled cultures.
Some place it near the start of the Holocene, as early peoples cleared forests, hunted megafauna to extinction and spread invasive species.

contested_note: Researchers propose start dates ranging from early farming to the 1950s.

definition.text: A name for the present age in which ecosystems worldwide grow more alike, mainly because people move species around the globe.

facts.text: Species are spread on purpose, as crops and livestock, or by accident.
The term was first used by Michael Samways in 1999.

definition.text: Assimilative capacity is how much pollution an environment can absorb without harm to it or to the people who use it.

facts.text: Nature absorbs pollutants by diluting and dispersing them and removing them through chemical or biological processes.
A pollutant actually causes pollution once the assimilative capacity is exceeded.
Fast-moving or large bodies of water can absorb more than a slow stream, because dilution is the main way water lowers contaminant levels.
If an irrigation standard for salt is 450 mg/L, a water body's assimilative capacity is the salt that can be added before that level is passed.
Governments use it as a guide for sustainable growth of city regions and to judge how much pressure a region is under.
It is criticised for a vague definition and for wrongly implying that small amounts of pollution do no harm.

definition.text: The rate at which waste can be added to a body of water while keeping contaminants below levels that cause unacceptable biological harm.

facts.text: It was proposed as a less ambiguous alternative to assimilative capacity because its uses are defined more in numbers.
Inconsistency in assimilative capacity led NOAA and the EPA to restrict that term.

definition.text: The biosphere is the sum of all the world's ecosystems: the zone of life on Earth.

facts.text: For matter it is almost a closed system, but for energy it is open, with photosynthesis capturing sunlight at around 100 terawatts.
It integrates all living things and their links with rock, ice, water and air.
Life is found everywhere from the polar ice caps to the equator, including at least 19 km underground and at least 64 km up in the atmosphere.
The term was coined in 1875 by geologist Eduard Suess; Vladimir Vernadsky gave it its ecological meaning in the 1920s.
Earth's biosphere is divided into biomes; most of the richest ones lie near the equator.

definition.text: Environmental degradation is the worsening of the environment through loss of resources such as clean air, water and soil, destruction of ecosystems and habitats, extinction of wildlife, and pollution.

facts.text: The UN disaster-reduction body defines it as reducing the environment's capacity to meet social and ecological needs.
Some degradation is plainly visible, like deforestation; some builds slowly, like plastic pollution or greenhouse gases pushing the climate toward tipping points.
Since farming began over 11,000 years ago, people have altered about 70% of Earth's land surface and halved the global mass of vegetation.
A 2021 study found just 3% of Earth's land is ecologically and faunally intact.
Its scale depends not only on population growth but also on consumption patterns and how efficiently resources are used.
Industrialised nations, with higher consumption per person, often have a disproportionately large environmental footprint.
Women's livelihoods, health, food security and access to water and energy are disproportionately hurt by it.

definition.text: The using up and spoiling of Earth's limited fresh water, a major part of environmental degradation.

facts.text: Only about 2.5% of Earth's water is fresh, and only 30% of that is available for use, since 69% is frozen in ice caps.
About 85% of freshwater consumption goes to irrigation of farmland, golf courses and parks.
An estimated one in three people worldwide already face water shortages.

definition.text: A UN term for three linked global environmental crises: pollution, climate change and biodiversity loss.

facts.text: The three crises feed one another, raising environmental risks and causing global economic loss.
Pollution is the leading environmental cause of disease and death; an estimated 9 million premature deaths in 2015 were linked to it.
The climate crisis comes from too much greenhouse gas in the atmosphere and brings rising temperatures, sea-level rise and extreme weather.
Up to one million plant and animal species face extinction, weakening ecosystems' ability to function and adapt.
Over half of global GDP depends on nature, and over 1 billion people's livelihoods are tied to forests.
The framework resembles other broad views of human impact, such as planetary boundaries.

definition.text: Short-termism is favouring quick profits and short-term results over long-term results and far-sighted action.

facts.text: It is linked to present bias, a thinking habit that prefers short-term payoffs to long-term rewards.
It can undermine actions whose results take longer than one government's term to appear.
Short-termism and consumerism are named among the barriers to sustainability.

title: Eco-capitalism

definition.text: Eco-capitalism, or green capitalism, is the view that nature is a form of capital on which all wealth depends, so markets should be used to solve environmental problems.

facts.text: It argues governments should use market-based tools such as a carbon tax.
A central aim is to correct the market failure in which polluters do not pay for the pollution they cause.
Critics such as eco-socialists say growth and the commodification of nature cannot easily be reconciled with sustainability.

contested_note: Critics argue that commodifying nature and pursuing growth cannot easily coexist with sustainability.

definition.text: Managing the oceans, fresh water, land and atmosphere at global scale according to sustainability principles.

facts.text: Changes in how land is split between cities, farms, forest and pasture strongly affect the global water, carbon and nitrogen cycles.
Biodiversity loss stems largely from habitat loss as natural capital is converted into man-made capital.
Since the Neolithic Revolution, human consumption has cut the world's forest cover by about 47%.
Feeding humanity takes about 38% of Earth's land surface and about 20% of its net primary productivity.

definition.text: The Dasgupta Review sorts capital goods into produced capital, human capital and natural capital.

facts.text: Economists confine the word capital to assets that are measurable, and the range has widened over time.
Roads, buildings, machines, ports and patents are tangible or intangible but alienable, and together are called produced capital.
Health, education and skills are intangible and non-alienable assets that together form human capital, included because ways to measure their value to individuals and society were found.
Natural capital became a third category once methods existed to measure the value people place on natural resources.
Natural capital ranges from plants (tangible and alienable) to pollinators, a sea view and the global climate (intangible and non-alienable).

The Review stresses the wedge between market prices of capital goods, especially natural capital, and their accounting or shadow prices, the contribution an extra unit makes to the flow of social benefits.
Many kinds of natural capital have no market and are free to the user, so special methods are needed to estimate accounting prices.
Mainstream growth and development theories, and the models used by finance ministries and central banks, leave out humanity's dependence on Nature.

title: Own rate of return on assets
article: pdf>dasgupta-review/The_Economics_of_Biodiversity_The_Dasgupta_Review_Full_Report.pdf#1.2 Rates of Return and Arbitrage Conditions

definition.text: An asset's yield, or own rate of return, is the growth expected tomorrow if one more unit of it is added to a portfolio today.

facts.text: For produced capital the yield is its marginal product; for a fishery or a tree it is the growth in biomass obtained by waiting.
Investment can be passive: restoring a wetland is investment, and so is conservation, which can simply mean waiting.
Yield is a pure number per unit of time; the UK government's long-term bonds have historically averaged about 4% a year, though more recently closer to 1%.
Because relative prices change unless the economy is stationary, own rates are not enough: the rate of return on an asset is its yield plus its capital gains over a unit of time.

definition.text: Nature does not maximise net primary production (NPP) or the regeneration rate of its ecosystems, even though a portfolio manager would try to maximise yield.

facts.text: NPP per square metre differs by biome: 0.75 kg a year in temperate grassland, 2.5 in tropical rainforest and 0.14 in the ocean, because the abiotic environment varies.
Nature does not maximise planetary NPP even after allowing for uneven abiotic conditions, and NPP in old growth forests is nearly zero.
Life-form distributions emerged under selection pressures at the genetic level and are not an efficient distribution of NPP.
In the Review's fishery example, yield is zero at the long-run population K, so the marginal product of the fish stock there is negative.

title: Invisibility of regulating services
article: pdf>dasgupta-review/The_Economics_of_Biodiversity_The_Dasgupta_Review_Full_Report.pdf#2.5 Invisibility and Silence of Regulating and

definition.text: Regulating and maintenance services are mostly hidden from view and silent, felt only over the long run or when they are lost.

facts.text: Provisioning and cultural services have readily detectable outcomes that are felt even in the short run.
Mangroves yield visible timber and fish, but their protection of villages against storms is appreciated only after they are degraded, and is far harder to value.
A study of the 1999 Orissa super-cyclone found that villages protected by more mangroves suffered less property damage.
The social cost of shrimp should include the carbon sequestered by the mangroves cleared for shrimp farms and the protection they gave nearby communities.

title: Mobility and silence of nature as a source of externalities
article: pdf>dasgupta-review/The_Economics_of_Biodiversity_The_Dasgupta_Review_Full_Report.pdf#1.7 Institutions and the Character of Natural Capital

definition.text: Externalities arise from the biosphere because property rights to large parts of it are weakly defined or enforced, and Nature is mobile, silent and invisible.

facts.text: An externality is an unaccounted-for consequence of one person's actions for others, including future people.
No one can contain the air they foul or the rivers they pollute, and the harm is non-excludable.
Pollution such as nitrogen and phosphorus in an estuary aggregates leakages from innumerable distant fields, factories and households, so polluters do not pay for using it as a sink.
No property rights cover the oceans beyond national jurisdiction, so no one has an incentive to protect them from contamination or overfishing.
Public goods are non-rivalrous and non-excludable, a mirror image of open access resources, and are underproduced for the same reason that open access resources are overused.

definition.text: The Dasgupta Review compares humanity's demand for the biosphere's goods and services with the biosphere's regeneration rate: when demand exceeds it, the biosphere depreciates.

facts.text: It builds on Ehrlich and Holdren's 1971 decomposition of impact into population, individual demands and the technologies and institutions in play.
Humanity's demand per unit of time, which Ehrlich and Holdren called impact, is today known as the global ecological footprint.
Demand takes two forms: harvesting goods and services for consumption and production, and using the biosphere as a sink for waste.
Both extraction X and waste Z are functions of population times income per capita, divided by efficiency terms: X = Ny/alpha_X and Z = Ny/alpha_Z.
Income per capita is used as a proxy for human activity, though it almost surely understates it.
Over the long run, global demand must equal the biosphere's capacity to supply it sustainably; uncovering this relation is the core of the Review.

definition.text: The Dasgupta Review distinguishes inequality in household incomes from inequality in households' impact on the biosphere, which is income corrected for the efficiency of converting nature into income.

facts.text: Households differ in income and in the efficiency with which they convert the biosphere's goods and services into income.
A household's income divided by its efficiency (y/alpha) can be read as its ecological footprint.
Across 136 countries the Review estimates footprint I = 0.97 y^0.41, where y is income per capita.
The global ecological footprint would be higher than today's if everyone received an equal share of today's global income.
